GreatXML staging — unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml written to Windows Recovery partition AIInstallation High
Hunts for writes of the two XML primitives named in the GreatXML disclosure (unattend.xml and ReAgent.xml) anywhere outside the canonical sysprep / recovery template locations. A drop of either file on a freshly-mounted recovery volume is the staging step before a Shift+Restart triggers WinRE to load the attacker's unattend manifest. Rationale: unattend.xml and Recovery/WindowsRE/ReAgent.xml are the two file primitives the Chaotic Eclipse write-up explicitly names as the staging payload — copying them to the root of the recovery partition is what causes WinRE to load attacker config on next boot. Excluding the three Microsoft-sanctioned hosts of those filenames (Panther/Sysprep/Recovery) keeps the FP set tiny.
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1564.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT imaging workflow refreshing the WinRE image via reagentc /setreimage from a UNC share
  • OEM (Dell/HP/Lenovo) factory-reset utility rebuilding the recovery partition
  • SCCM/Intune task sequence re-deploying an unattend.xml during PXE provisioning
  • Sysprep generalize step writing unattend.xml to a non-standard staging path before move
  • Backup product mounting the recovery volume and copying its contents for an image
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sysprep.exe", "setupcl.exe", "reagentc.exe", "dism.exe", "setup.exe")) | where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/generalize", "/oobe", "/setreimage", "/apply-image"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the initiating process and account; pull the SHA256 of the dropped XML and check whether the path is on the system drive (legit re-imaging) vs a separately-mounted volume with no drive letter pre-event (GreatXML staging). Confirm the user is not in the imaging/IT-build security group. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host from the network, suspend the user's session, snapshot the recovery partition before reboot, and disable Defender Offline Scan triggering via Group Policy until the host is rebuilt. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessAccountSid for any diskpart/mountvol/reagentc activity in the prior 24h, sweep for the same SHA256 across the fleet, and check for Start-MpWDOScan in PowerShell logs which is the precondition the researcher names.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "unattend.xml" or FileName =~ "ReAgent.xml"
| where not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\Panther\")
| where not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\Sysprep\")
| where not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\Recovery\")
| where not(InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where TargetFileName =~ "unattend.xml" or TargetFileName =~ "ReAgent.xml"
| where not(TargetFilePath has @"\Windows\Panther\")
| where not(TargetFilePath has @"\Windows\System32\Sysprep\")
| where not(TargetFilePath has @"\Windows\System32\Recovery\")
| where not(ActorUsername endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Recovery Partition Configuration XML Written Outside Standard Paths
id: a8f5c4d1-2b3e-4f6a-9d7c-1e2f3a4b5c6d
description: Detects creation of unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml outside the canonical Windows sysprep / recovery template paths. Used by the GreatXML BitLocker bypass to stage an attacker-controlled unattend manifest on the recovery partition.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1542.003
  - attack.t1564.005
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\unattend.xml'
      - '\ReAgent.xml'
  filter_legit:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\Windows\Panther\'
      - '\Windows\System32\Sysprep\'
      - '\Windows\System32\Recovery\'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate Sysprep / unattended Windows setup imaging
  - WinRE re-imaging via reagentc /setreimage to a vendor share
  - OEM recovery tooling refreshing the recovery image
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\unattend.xml OR *\\Unattend.xml OR *\\UNATTEND.XML OR *\\ReAgent.xml OR *\\reagent.xml OR *\\REAGENT.XML) -@TargetFilename:(*\\Windows\\Panther\\* OR *\\Windows\\System32\\Sysprep\\* OR *\\Windows\\System32\\Recovery\\*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(unattend|reagent)\.xml$/i
| NOT TargetFileName=/\\Windows\\(Panther|System32\\Sysprep|System32\\Recovery)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name=unattend.xml OR Filesystem.file_name=ReAgent.xml) AND Filesystem.action=created AND NOT (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Windows\\Panther\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Windows\\System32\\Sysprep\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Windows\\System32\\Recovery\\*") AND NOT Filesystem.user="*$" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name=unattend.xml OR Filesystem.file_name=ReAgent.xml) AND Filesystem.action=created AND NOT (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Windows\\Panther\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Windows\\System32\\Sysprep\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Windows\\System32\\Recovery\\*") AND NOT Filesystem.user="*$" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Recovery partition exposure — diskpart/mountvol assigning letter to hidden WinRE volume AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts for the prerequisite action that lets an attacker write the GreatXML payload: mounting the normally-hidden recovery partition to a drive letter via diskpart scripts, mountvol against a \\?\Volume{} GUID, or reagentc /setreimage. Without this step, the unattend.xml/ReAgent.xml drop in UC1 isn't reachable. Rationale: The recovery partition is hidden (no drive letter) by default — the only way to land files there is to mount it first. diskpart 'assign letter' inside a script, mountvol against a \\?\Volume{GUID} path, or reagentc /setreimage are the three Windows-native mechanisms. Suppressing imaging-tool parents removes the dominant FP class.
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MDT/SCCM task sequence mounting recovery during OSD
  • OEM (Dell SupportAssist, HP Recovery Manager) refreshing the WinRE image
  • Sysadmin running reagentc /setreimage to repair a broken WinRE.wim
  • Backup software (Veeam, Acronis) mounting the recovery volume to image it
  • User following a Microsoft KB to recreate WinRE after a failed feature update
Suppression filter
| where not(IsInitiatingProcessRemoteSession == true and AccountName has "imaging") | where not(InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("tsmanager.exe", "tsbootshell.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full diskpart script (often passed via /s scriptfile) or the mountvol target GUID; correlate to whether the host is in an active OS-deployment collection. Confirm the parent isn't an imaging engine (smsts.exe, sccm.exe). Step 2 — Contain: if the parent is a user shell (explorer.exe, cmd.exe spawned from outlook/teams) and the account isn't in IT, isolate the host immediately — the next step in the GreatXML chain is the XML drop. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot from this event to UC1's DeviceFileEvents on the same DeviceId in the +30 minute window; check for Start-MpWDOScan PowerShell activity by the same account in the prior 24 hours (the article-named precondition).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("diskpart.exe", "mountvol.exe", "reagentc.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("assign letter", "select partition", "/setreimage", " /s ", "Volume{")
| where not(InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sccm.exe", "smsts.exe", "dism.exe", "sysprep.exe", "setup.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("diskpart.exe", "mountvol.exe", "reagentc.exe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("assign letter", "select partition", "/setreimage", " /s ", "Volume{")
| where not(ActorUsername endswith "$")
| where not(ActingProcessName in~ ("sccm.exe", "smsts.exe", "dism.exe", "sysprep.exe", "setup.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Recovery Partition Mount or WinRE Configuration Tooling
id: b9e6d5c2-3c4f-5a7b-ae8d-2f3a4b5c6d7e
description: Detects diskpart, mountvol or reagentc invocations assigning a drive letter to the hidden Windows recovery partition or rewriting the WinRE image pointer. Required precondition for the GreatXML BitLocker bypass to land its unattend.xml payload.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1542.003
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\diskpart.exe'
      - '\mountvol.exe'
      - '\reagentc.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'assign letter'
      - 'select partition'
      - '/setreimage'
      - 'Volume{'
  filter_imaging:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\sccm.exe'
      - '\smsts.exe'
      - '\dism.exe'
      - '\sysprep.exe'
      - '\setup.exe'
  condition: selection_img and selection_cmd and not filter_imaging
falsepositives:
  - SCCM/MDT task sequences that mount the recovery partition during OS deployment
  - OEM recovery refresh utilities
  - Sysadmin troubleshooting a broken WinRE image
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\diskpart.exe OR *\\Diskpart.exe OR *\\DiskPart.exe OR *\\mountvol.exe OR *\\MountVol.exe OR *\\reagentc.exe OR *\\ReAgentc.exe OR *\\ReAgentC.exe) @CommandLine:(*"assign letter"* OR *"select partition"* OR *"/setreimage"* OR *"Volume{"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(diskpart|mountvol|reagentc)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(assign\\s+letter|select\\s+partition|/setreimage|Volume\\{)", field=CommandLine)
| NOT ParentBaseFileName=/(sccm|smsts|dism|sysprep|setup)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

GreatXML chain — recovery partition mount followed by ReAgent.xml/unattend.xml drop within 30 minutes AIInstallation High
High-fidelity temporal correlation that joins UC2 (recovery partition mount) with UC1 (unattend/ReAgent XML drop) on the same host inside a 30-minute window. This is the exact GreatXML pre-boot staging sequence described by Chaotic Eclipse and the only combination that warrants page-out alerting. Rationale: The article describes a strict two-step sequence: (1) make the recovery partition addressable, then (2) drop unattend.xml + Recovery\WindowsRE\ReAgent.xml at its root. Either event alone is noisy (imaging workflows); the two together within minutes on one host is the GreatXML signature and is essentially zero-FP outside an active OS-deployment task sequence.
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1564.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SCCM/MDT OSD task sequence that mounts the recovery partition and writes a fresh unattend.xml during reimaging
  • OEM factory-reset utility refreshing both the partition mapping and the recovery manifest
  • IT engineer manually rebuilding a corrupted WinRE following the Microsoft KB
  • Backup product mounting the recovery volume and writing audit metadata XMLs
  • DISM /Apply-Image redeploying a captured WIM including these XMLs
Suppression filter
| where not(MountParent in~ ("smsts.exe", "tsmanager.exe", "sccm.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "dism.exe", "sysprep.exe")) | where not(DropProcess in~ ("smsts.exe", "dism.exe", "setupprep.exe", "sysprep.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull both processes (mount + drop) and confirm the user is not a member of the IT/imaging security group; check whether SCCM CcmExec is the grandparent (legitimate OSD). Capture SHA256 of the dropped XML and compare to the in-box C:\Windows\System32\Recovery\ReAgent.xml. Step 2 — Contain: page on-call, isolate the host BEFORE the user can reboot, suspend the BitLocker volume protector key escrow until forensics complete, and capture a live memory image — the WinRE shell from a follow-up boot will have direct access to the unlocked volume. Step 3 — Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same DroppedSha256, query any host where the same AccountName ran Start-MpWDOScan in the prior 24h, and confirm no other host shows a UC1 hit on the dropped XML.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let CorrelationWindow = 30m;
let PartitionMount = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileName in~ ("diskpart.exe", "mountvol.exe", "reagentc.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("assign letter", "select partition", "/setreimage", "Volume{")
    | where not(InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
    | project MountTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, MountCmd = ProcessCommandLine, MountParent = InitiatingProcessFileName;
let XmlDrop = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
    | where FileName =~ "unattend.xml" or FileName =~ "ReAgent.xml"
    | where not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\Panther\")
    | where not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\Sysprep\")
    | where not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\Recovery\")
    | project DropTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DroppedPath = FolderPath, DroppedFile = FileName, DropProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, DroppedSha256 = SHA256;
PartitionMount
| join kind=inner XmlDrop on DeviceId
| where DropTime between (MountTime .. MountTime + CorrelationWindow)
| extend DelayMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', DropTime, MountTime)
| project MountTime, DropTime, DelayMinutes, DeviceName, AccountName, MountCmd, MountParent, DroppedPath, DroppedFile, DropProcess, DroppedSha256
| order by MountTime desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let CorrelationWindow = 30m;
let PartitionMount = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where TargetProcessName has_any ("diskpart.exe", "mountvol.exe", "reagentc.exe")
    | where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("assign letter", "select partition", "/setreimage", "Volume{")
    | where not(ActorUsername endswith "$")
    | project MountTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, MountCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, MountParent = ActingProcessName;
let XmlDrop = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where EventType in~ ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
    | where TargetFileName =~ "unattend.xml" or TargetFileName =~ "ReAgent.xml"
    | where not(TargetFilePath has @"\Windows\Panther\")
    | where not(TargetFilePath has @"\Windows\System32\Sysprep\")
    | where not(TargetFilePath has @"\Windows\System32\Recovery\")
    | project DropTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DroppedPath = TargetFilePath, DroppedFile = TargetFileName, DropProcess = ActingProcessName, DroppedSha256 = TargetFileSHA256;
PartitionMount
| join kind=inner XmlDrop on DvcHostname
| where DropTime between (MountTime .. MountTime + CorrelationWindow)
| extend DelayMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', DropTime, MountTime)
| project MountTime, DropTime, DelayMinutes, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, MountCmd, MountParent, DroppedPath, DroppedFile, DropProcess, DroppedSha256
| order by MountTime desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(diskpart|mountvol|reagentc)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(assign\\s+letter|select\\s+partition|/setreimage|Volume\\{)", field=CommandLine)
| MountTime := @timestamp
| join({#event_simpleName=FileWritten | TargetFileName=/(unattend|reagent)\.xml$/i | NOT TargetFileName=/\\Windows\\(Panther|System32\\Sysprep|System32\\Recovery)\\/i | DropTime := @timestamp | groupBy([aid], function={ selectLast([DropTime, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName]) })}, field=aid, include=[DropTime, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName])
| DropTime > MountTime
| (DropTime - MountTime) < 1800000
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=collect([MountTime, DropTime, CommandLine, TargetFileName]))

ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)

| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45585")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

DeviceProcessEvents

[GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-48062: CodeIgniter4 has a validation bypass when uploading file extensions via `ext_in` rule

GitHub Security Advisories
2026-06-11 4 use cases 1 technique 4 kill-chain phases detected

CodeIgniter4 has a validation bypass when uploading file extensions via `ext_in` rule

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Multipart upload: image Content-Type with PHP/PHAR filename extension to CodeIgniter4 endpoint
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Webserver/PHP worker spawns shell or recon binary from CodeIgniter4 host
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Webserver process writes PHP/PHAR script into CodeIgniter4 upload directory

Webserver process writes PHP/PHAR script into CodeIgniter4 upload directory AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-bypass artifact of CVE-2026-48062: a webserver/PHP worker (php-fpm, php-cgi, httpd, nginx, w3wp, caddy, apache2) writing a file whose extension is .php/.phar/.phtml/.phps into directories that match CodeIgniter4 upload conventions (uploads, writable/uploads, public). The ext_in rule on the affected versions accepts these because MIME guess says gif/png/jpeg, but the on-disk filename retains the executable extension via $file->move($path) — so this file-create event is the moment the webshell lands. Rationale: Detection anchors on the article's exact end state — '$file->move($path) ... store uploads in a web-accessible directory ... allow PHP files to run from that directory'. The combination (PHP worker process writing .php/.phar/.phtml/.phps into uploads|writable/uploads|public path) is unambiguously the dropped webshell from the ext_in bypass; legitimate PHP apps never write executable .php into uploads at runtime. Cross-checked the CWE-434 reference and CodeIgniter4 upload docs cited in the advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://codeigniter.com/user_guide/libraries/uploaded_files.html • https://codeigniter.com/user_guide/libraries/validation.html#rules-for-file-uploads • https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/434.html • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Composer install writing vendor PHP files into a publicly-mounted folder (e.g. composer update on a misconfigured deployment that maps vendor/ into public/)
  • CMS/plugin auto-updater (Drupal/Symfony bundle install) writing .php files into public/ during a maintenance window
  • Developer using a deploy script that staging-copies .php files into uploads/ for testing image-handler routes
  • Caching modules (e.g. opcache warmers) creating .php files under writable/cache when misrouted to writable/uploads
  • Backup/restore tooling unpacking a tarball that contains .php under uploads/
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer", "--update", "artisan", "deploy.sh") and FolderPath has "vendor")
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the SHA256 of the dropped file; fetch the file contents via DeviceFile/Live Response. Look for GIF89a/GIF87a magic followed by <?php or <? tags (the polyglot payload described in the advisory). Check whether CodeIgniter4 framework version on the host is < 4.7.3. 2) Contain — isolate the host from the network if the file content confirms a webshell; quarantine the dropped file; rotate any credentials/secrets readable from the upload directory or webserver process environment. 3) Hunt — pivot on the webserver process PID to enumerate child processes (UC2), search the same upload path for other recently-created .php files, and review web access logs for GET requests to the file path within the last 30 days to scope attacker interaction.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php-fpm.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","w3wp.exe","caddy.exe","apache2.exe")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/](uploads|writable[\\/]uploads|public)[\\/]"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(php|phar|phtml|phps)$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(php-fpm|php-cgi|httpd|nginx|w3wp|caddy|apache2)(\.exe)?$"
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/](uploads|writable[\\/]uploads|public)[\\/]"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phar","phtml","phps")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          TargetFileExtension, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Webserver process writes PHP/PHAR script into upload directory (CVE-2026-48062)
id: 2c4a8e76-91d2-4f5b-ae18-3d57cae4061a
description: Detects PHP/web worker writing an executable-PHP-extension file into a CodeIgniter4-style upload path, the post-bypass artifact of the ext_in MIME-vs-extension validation flaw in CodeIgniter4 < 4.7.3.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx
  - https://codeigniter.com/user_guide/libraries/validation.html
  - https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/434.html
author: SOC Pipeline
date: 2026/06/18
tags:

logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\php-fpm.exe'
      - '\php-cgi.exe'
      - '\httpd.exe'
      - '\nginx.exe'
      - '\w3wp.exe'
      - '\caddy.exe'
      - '\apache2.exe'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\uploads\'
      - '\writable\uploads\'
      - '\public\'
      - '/uploads/'
      - '/writable/uploads/'
      - '/public/'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.php'
      - '.phar'
      - '.phtml'
      - '.phps'
  condition: all of selection_*
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate CMS/plugin auto-update writing .php files to public/ during maintenance
  - Developer composer install writing vendor PHP files to publicly-mounted paths
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\php-cgi.exe OR *\\php-fpm.exe OR *\\httpd.exe OR *\\nginx.exe OR *\\w3wp.exe OR *\\caddy.exe OR *\\PHP-FPM.exe OR *\\W3WP.exe) (@TargetFilename:*\\uploads\\*.php OR @TargetFilename:*\\uploads\\*.phar OR @TargetFilename:*\\uploads\\*.phtml OR @TargetFilename:*\\writable\\uploads\\*.php OR @TargetFilename:*\\public\\*.php OR @TargetFilename:*\\public\\*.phtml)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/(php-fpm|php-cgi|httpd|nginx|w3wp|caddy|apache2)(\.exe)?$/i TargetFileName=/[\\\/](uploads|writable[\\\/]uploads|public)[\\\/].+\.(php|phar|phtml|phps)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
| sort(count, order=desc)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created AND Filesystem.process_name IN ("php-cgi.exe","php-fpm.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","w3wp.exe","caddy.exe","apache2","apache2.exe") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\uploads\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/uploads/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/writable/uploads/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\writable\\uploads\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/public/*") AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.php" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.phar" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.phtml" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.phps") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created AND Filesystem.process_name IN ("php-cgi.exe","php-fpm.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","w3wp.exe","caddy.exe","apache2","apache2.exe") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\uploads\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/uploads/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/writable/uploads/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\writable\\uploads\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/public/*") AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.php" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.phar" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.phtml" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.phps") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Multipart upload: image Content-Type with PHP/PHAR filename extension to CodeIgniter4 endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the ingress signal of CVE-2026-48062: an HTTP POST multipart upload to a CodeIgniter4 upload endpoint where the request's Content-Type is image/* but the multipart filename field carries .php/.phar/.phtml/.phps. Because the ext_in rule trusts the MIME-guessed extension, this exact combination is the exploit attempt. Correlates the POST with a subsequent GET to a .php under the upload tree as the high-confidence pivot to confirm execution. Rationale: The advisory's worked example — uploaded[avatar]|is_image[avatar]|mime_in[avatar,image/gif]|ext_in[avatar,gif] — pins the vulnerable endpoint shape to URI tokens (avatar, upload, profile, image) and the post-exploit access shape to GET on .php under uploads/. The POST→GET correlation within 30 minutes mirrors how attackers verify the dropped webshell after a successful bypass. Defender query intentionally left as a comment because DeviceNetworkEvents lacks HTTP body/Content-Type fields needed for the multipart-mismatch check; pointing at the dedicated web-access tables is the honest answer. Cross-checked against: • https://codeigniter.com/user_guide/libraries/validation.html#rules-for-file-uploads • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1036.008
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate avatar upload followed by user previewing their profile page that happens to reference a .php profile renderer in the same path tree
  • Image gallery thumbnailer that re-fetches uploaded images via PHP rendering endpoints under /uploads/render.php
  • Vulnerability scanners (Burp, Acunetix) sweeping multipart endpoints and then GET-probing /uploads/ for known webshell names
  • CMS admin uploading a plugin .phar through a /admin/upload endpoint as part of routine maintenance
  • Profile image cropping flow where the cropper UI POSTs the cropped image then GETs a templated PHP processor URL
Suppression filter
| where not (csUserAgent has_any ("Burp","Acunetix","Nessus","Nikto","sqlmap") and cIP in (dynamic(["<known scanner IPs>"])))
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the raw multipart body (if WAF/proxy preserves it) and confirm the filename field ends in .php/.phar while Content-Type is image/*. Examine the GET response body for shell artifacts (`<?php`, eval, system, base64_decode). 2) Contain — block the source IP at the WAF/edge; pull the dropped file from the upload directory and quarantine; if CodeIgniter4 < 4.7.3 is in use, prioritize patch deployment or apply the workaround ($file->getRandomName() / move uploads outside web root). 3) Hunt — replay the source IP through 30-day access logs looking for other suspicious POSTs to upload endpoints; search peer hosts for the same upload-then-execute pattern; review codebase for all uses of ext_in and confirm the fix from advisory v4.7.3 is applied.
// Defender DeviceNetworkEvents does not expose HTTP method, Content-Type or multipart body.
// This detection cannot be expressed on native Defender Advanced Hunting tables — point at IIS/Apache/Nginx access logs in Sentinel/Splunk/Datadog instead.
let Window = 30m;
let UploadPosts = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csMethod == "POST"
    | where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/(upload|avatar|profile|attachment|image|file)"
    | where scStatus < 400
    | project PostTime = TimeGenerated, cIP, Computer, PostUri = csUriStem, csUserAgent;
let PhpHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csMethod == "GET"
    | where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)\.(php|phar|phtml|phps)$"
    | where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/(uploads|writable|public)/"
    | project GetTime = TimeGenerated, cIP, Computer, GetUri = csUriStem, scStatus;
UploadPosts
| join kind=inner PhpHits on cIP, Computer
| where GetTime between (PostTime .. PostTime + Window)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', GetTime, PostTime)
| project PostTime, GetTime, DelaySec, cIP, Computer, PostUri, GetUri, csUserAgent, scStatus
| order by PostTime desc
(source:nginx.access OR source:apache.access OR source:iis) @http.method:POST (@http.url_details.path:*upload* OR @http.url_details.path:*avatar* OR @http.url_details.path:*profile* OR @http.url_details.path:*attachment*) @http.status_code:[200 TO 299]
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="POST" AND (Web.url="*/upload*" OR Web.url="*/avatar*" OR Web.url="*/profile*" OR Web.url="*/attachment*" OR Web.url="*/image*") by Web.dest Web.src Web.url Web.http_user_agent _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | rename _time as post_time, url as post_url | join type=inner dest src [| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="GET" AND (Web.url="*.php*" OR Web.url="*.phar*" OR Web.url="*.phtml*") AND (Web.url="*/uploads/*" OR Web.url="*/writable/*" OR Web.url="*/public/*") by Web.dest Web.src Web.url _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | rename _time as get_time, url as get_url] | where get_time >= post_time AND (get_time - post_time) <= 1800 | table post_time, get_time, src, dest, post_url, get_url, http_user_agent
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="POST" AND (Web.url="*/upload*" OR Web.url="*/avatar*" OR Web.url="*/profile*" OR Web.url="*/attachment*" OR Web.url="*/image*") by Web.dest Web.src Web.url Web.http_user_agent _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | rename _time as post_time, url as post_url | join type=inner dest src [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="GET" AND (Web.url="*.php*" OR Web.url="*.phar*" OR Web.url="*.phtml*") AND (Web.url="*/uploads/*" OR Web.url="*/writable/*" OR Web.url="*/public/*") by Web.dest Web.src Web.url _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | rename _time as get_time, url as get_url] | where get_time >= post_time AND (get_time - post_time) <= 1800 | table post_time, get_time, src, dest, post_url, get_url, http_user_agent
Webserver/PHP worker spawns shell or recon binary from CodeIgniter4 host AIExploitation High
Hunts the execution stage after a successful CVE-2026-48062 webshell drop: php-fpm/php-cgi/httpd/nginx/w3wp/apache2 process spawning cmd, powershell, bash, sh, whoami, wget, curl, net, tasklist, systeminfo, nc, ncat, certutil, or wmic. The webserver process rarely needs these binaries during normal request handling; this parent-child shape is the canonical 'webshell executed a system command' signal called out by the OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet referenced in the advisory. Rationale: The advisory states the outcome is 'arbitrary code execution' from a PHP file rendered in a web-accessible directory — the operational signal of that execution is the webserver process forking a non-PHP child. Parent-child pair (php-fpm/httpd/nginx/w3wp → cmd/powershell/whoami/curl/wget/net/...) is one of the highest-fidelity webshell post-exploit detections per the OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet referenced from the GHSA. Cross-checked against: • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html • https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/434.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application using exec()/proc_open() to call whoami or hostname for diagnostics in a /status endpoint
  • Deployment pipeline running curl from a php-fpm worker as part of a release-trigger callback
  • Liveness probe that has the webserver invoke 'powershell Get-Service' on Windows health checks
  • Legacy CMS plugin using exec('certutil -hashfile ...') for file integrity verification
  • Monitoring agent injected via composer that shells out to systeminfo/tasklist for telemetry
Suppression filter
| where not (CommandLine has_any ("-Command Get-Service","hostname","--version") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("http://","https://","-enc","DownloadString","IEX"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — capture the parent php-fpm/httpd/nginx process command line and the child's full command line including arguments; pull the recent HTTP access logs for that host filtered to .php/.phar GETs in the last hour to find which uploaded webshell was invoked. 2) Contain — kill the child process, isolate the host, and rotate the webserver account/service-principal credentials; remove the dropped webshell file identified in UC1. 3) Hunt — search 30 days of process telemetry for the same parent-child pair across the fleet; check egress connections from the webserver process to public IPs (uncommon outside of API integrations); verify CodeIgniter4 framework version is upgraded to >= 4.7.3 on all affected hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php-fpm.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","w3wp.exe","caddy.exe","apache2.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","wget.exe","curl.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","tasklist.exe","systeminfo.exe","nc.exe","ncat.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wmic.exe","certutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(php-fpm|php-cgi|httpd|nginx|w3wp|caddy|apache2)\.exe$"
| where NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|whoami|wget|curl|net|net1|tasklist|systeminfo|nc|ncat|bash|sh|wmic|certutil)\.exe$"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, SubjectUserName,
          ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Phantom Gyp: small binding.gyp written into node_modules during npm install · [LLM] Editor/AI tool auto-execute config file dropped into project tree by package manager or git
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] VS Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini spawns interpreter referencing folderOpen or SessionStart hook script · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Miasma and Hades Are Spreading Now: Detect Them on Developer Machines with Suspi
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Miasma/Hades known-bad SHA256 execution on developer endpoint · [LLM] Hades on-import payload: python interpreter spawns Bun runtime download · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Bun runtime egress to npm/PyPI publish endpoints or attacker-controlled GitHub repos
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Miasma/Hades known-bad SHA256 execution on developer endpoint AIInstallation Medium
Alerts when any of the 5 SHA256 hashes associated with the Miasma/Hades June 2026 campaign are observed as either an executed binary or a file written to disk on an enrolled host. Catches the worm landing or running irrespective of the delivery vector (npm install, IDE folder open, PyPI import). Rationale: Uses the 5 SHA256 IOCs pre-extracted from the StepSecurity advisory. Cross-checked against Semgrep's Miasma v2 writeup and StepSecurity's Hades campaign writeup which confirm the same hash family. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/the-hades-campaign-pypi-packages • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating IOC in a sandbox VM enrolled to production tenant
  • Defender threat-intel sample auto-downloaded to MpCmdRun quarantine folder
  • Forensic analyst copying the sample to a triage share for review
  • SOAR enrichment pipeline storing the binary in an evidence bucket synced back to disk
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Scans\" and FolderPath !has "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !has "\\evidence\\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the host's last 24h DeviceProcessEvents/DeviceFileEvents and confirm whether the hash was executed (process row) or only landed (file row). Identify the parent (npm.exe, node-gyp, python.exe) and the originating package/folder path. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the device in Defender (Isolate Device), force-rotate any npm/PyPI/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure tokens that lived on that host or in any repo the developer recently opened — assume tokens were exfiltrated. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on AccountUpn across all hosts for the same hash, then hunt UC2/UC3 (Phantom Gyp + Hades Bun) against the same user/devices to map full scope; review GitHub for any new workflow files or attacker-controlled repos.

Phantom Gyp: small binding.gyp written into node_modules during npm install AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Miasma 'Phantom Gyp' technique: a ~157-byte binding.gyp file dropped into a package directory under node_modules that triggers code execution at the native build step of npm install, bypassing preinstall/postinstall script monitoring. Filters to package-manager parent processes so legitimate library development is not flagged. Rationale: Article explicitly names the 157-byte binding.gyp as the Phantom Gyp payload dropped during npm install. Size filter (50-500 bytes) plus the node_modules path plus the npm/yarn/pnpm parent are all article-derived; legitimate binding.gyp files in published packages are typically much larger and produced by the package author rather than dropped by tar extraction during install. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/ • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer authoring a genuinely tiny binding.gyp stub for a local native addon being tested under node_modules
  • tar.exe extracting a benign package whose author shipped a minimal binding.gyp (e.g. config-only)
  • pnpm content-addressable store unpacking many legitimate binding.gyp files during fresh install
  • Forensic analyst copying a malicious binding.gyp sample to a node_modules path for sandbox testing
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\node_modules\.pnpm\@types\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "npm publish" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp configure"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: open the file, read its content (it will be small JS/Python embedded inside the gyp action block), and identify the package directory it landed in. Capture the package name + version from the adjacent package.json. Step 2 — Contain: kill any running node-gyp / npm install on the host, isolate the device in EDR, and force-revoke the developer's NPM_TOKEN, GitHub PAT, AWS/Azure/GCP creds, and any tokens visible in process memory of the npm invocation. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the package name across the org to identify other developers who installed the same version; trigger UC1 hash search and UC6 Bun-exfil search; query npm registry for all versions of that package published in the last 7 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where FolderPath has @"\node_modules\"
| where FileSize between (50 .. 500)   // article: 157-byte Phantom Gyp; allow small obfuscation variance
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","tar.exe","7z.exe","git.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm i ","npm ci","yarn add","yarn install","pnpm install","pnpm add")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\"
| where TargetFileSize between (50 .. 500)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(npm|node|yarn|pnpm|tar|7z|git)\.exe$"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm i ","npm ci","yarn add","pnpm install")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
