git.exe spawned by node/npm — git dependency resolution path (npm 12 --allow-git default-off) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the second behaviour npm v12 is changing — Git dependency resolution. The article explicitly notes a Git dependency's .npmrc can override the Git executable even with `--ignore-scripts`. Detects node/npm spawning git.exe to clone/fetch, which after the upgrade should only happen with `--allow-git`. Rationale: Anchored on the article's `--allow-git` flag and the explicit warning that a Git dependency's `.npmrc` could override the Git executable even with `--ignore-scripts`. Parent=node/npm + child=git.exe + clone/fetch is the exact resolution path npm v12 blocks by default. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/configuring-npm/package-json#git-urls-as-dependencies
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Approved github:org/repo dependencies in package.json on developer machines
  • Release tooling running `npm pack <git-url>` during versioning
  • Yarn-to-npm migration scripts that resolve a temporary Git dep
  • Internal monorepo bootstrap that uses git submodules via npm
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the cloned Git URL from GitCmd — is it an approved internal org repo, or a third-party fork? Open the matching package.json/lockfile and confirm the dep was committed by a real engineer (not auto-bumped). 2) Contain: if the URL is suspicious, kill the build, rotate any tokens the runner held (npm, GitHub PAT), and block further installs until reviewed. 3) Hunt: search for git.exe spawned by node across the fleet in the last 30 days to catalogue every Git-resolved dep ahead of the npm 12 cutover; flag any whose .npmrc sets a custom `git` path.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe")
| where FileName =~ "git.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","fetch","ls-remote","archive")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GitCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "git.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("clone","fetch","ls-remote","archive")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

node-gyp rebuild execution — implicit native build path npm 12 blocks AIInstallation Medium
Article explicitly calls out that a package with a `binding.gyp` and no explicit install script still gets blocked because npm runs an implicit `node-gyp rebuild` for it. This hunts the rebuild process itself, surfacing every dependency that today relies on the implicit native-build path so engineers can pre-approve it before npm 12. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact wording — 'a package with a binding.gyp and no explicit install script still gets blocked, because npm runs an implicit node-gyp rebuild for it'. Inventorying these calls now lets engineering pre-approve them via `npm approve-scripts` before the npm 12 cutover. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nodejs/node-gyp
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine builds of bcrypt, sharp, node-sass, sqlite3, canvas, libxmljs — all use node-gyp legitimately
  • Fresh CI runners installing every dep from scratch trigger a rebuild for every native package
  • Electron apps rebuilding native modules against the electron headers on first install
  • Developer onboarding flows that nuke and reinstall node_modules
Suppression filter
| where PackagePath !in ("bcrypt","sharp","node-sass","sass","sqlite3","canvas","libxmljs","node-pty","node-expat","better-sqlite3")
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a survey hunt — treat the output as an inventory, not an alert. For each distinct PackagePath, confirm it's a known-good native dep the team relies on. 2) Contain: there's nothing to contain; the purpose is to feed the `npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending` workflow the article recommends before upgrading. 3) Hunt: cross-reference PackagePath against npm advisory feeds (osv.dev, GitHub Advisory Database) to spot any with recent supply-chain CVEs that should be removed rather than approved.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp rebuild","node-gyp configure","node-gyp build","binding.gyp")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend PackagePath = extract(@"node_modules[\\/]([^\\/]+)", 1, tostring(ProcessCommandLine))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Events=count(),
            Hosts=dcount(DeviceName), SampleCmd=any(ProcessCommandLine)
            by PackagePath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen asc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("node-gyp rebuild","node-gyp configure","node-gyp build","binding.gyp")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend PackagePath = extract(@"node_modules[\\/]([^\\/]+)", 1, tostring(CommandLine))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hosts=dcount(Computer), SampleCmd=any(CommandLine)
           by PackagePath, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName
| order by FirstSeen asc

.npmrc file write referencing custom git executable override AIInstallation Medium
Article calls out that a Git dependency's `.npmrc` could override the Git executable even with `--ignore-scripts`, providing a code execution path. Detects writes to `.npmrc` files whose contents set `git=` to a non-standard path or include shell-execution hooks — the override mechanism npm v12 closes by defaulting `--allow-git` to none. Rationale: Anchored on the article's specific statement that a Git dependency's `.npmrc` could override the Git executable as a code-execution path npm v12 closes. The high-fidelity pivot is a `.npmrc` written *inside node_modules* or by a non-developer process, which never happens in legitimate workflows. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/configuring-npm/npmrc
ATT&CKT1574 T1195.001 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running `npm config set` updating their personal ~/.npmrc (always outside node_modules)
  • CI runner provisioning a project-level .npmrc with registry auth tokens at the repo root
  • VS Code or JetBrains extensions writing a workspace-scoped .npmrc
  • Yarn/pnpm interoperability tools converting config files
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath endswith "\\Users\\" or FolderPath has "\\Users\\Public\\") and FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written .npmrc and look for `git=`, `script-shell=`, or any path under %APPDATA% / %TEMP%. A .npmrc inside node_modules pointing `git` at a custom binary is the smoking gun. 2) Contain: kill the install, delete the implanted .npmrc, isolate the host, and rotate any npm/GitHub tokens the workstation held. 3) Hunt: identify the parent package (FolderPath above node_modules), pull its tarball from the registry, and search the org's lockfiles for other consumers of the same package.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","git.exe","tar.exe","7z.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
   or FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          FolderPath, FileName, ActionType,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","git.exe","tar.exe","7z.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
   or TargetFilePath has "/node_modules/"
   or TargetFilePath has "\\node_modules\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: .npmrc written inside node_modules or by build tooling
id: 5f9b4a04-4444-4d44-9404-dd44dd44dd44
description: Detects writes to .npmrc within node_modules or by node/npm/git/archive utilities — the mechanism the article describes for overriding the git executable to gain code execution even when --ignore-scripts is set.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/11
tags:
  - attack.t1574
  - attack.t1195.001
  - attack.t1546
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\.npmrc'
  selection_context:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.cmd'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\git.exe'
      - '\tar.exe'
      - '\7z.exe'
  inside_node_modules:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\node_modules\'
  condition: selection_file and (selection_context or inside_node_modules)
falsepositives:
  - Developers running `npm config set` to update their personal ~/.npmrc (filter on FolderPath outside node_modules).
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\.npmrc OR *\.NPMRC) (@Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\npm.cmd OR *\npm.exe OR *\git.exe OR *\tar.exe OR *\7z.exe) OR @TargetFilename:*\node_modules\*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\\.npmrc$/i
| regex("\\\\node_modules\\\\", field=TargetFileName) OR ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|npm|git|tar|7z)\.(exe|cmd)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" (Filesystem.process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","git.exe","tar.exe","7z.exe")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" (Filesystem.process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","git.exe","tar.exe","7z.exe")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
node.exe outbound HTTPS to non-registry destination during npm install AICommand & Control Medium
Article's threat model is install-time code that runs arbitrary code — typical follow-on is contacting C2 or exfiltrating tokens. Detects node.exe / npm child processes initiating outbound HTTPS to anything that isn't the npm registry CDN, during the install window — the kind of egress legitimate package resolution doesn't make. Rationale: Anchored on the article's threat model — install scripts running 'arbitrary code on a developer machine or CI runner'. The high-signal pivot is the destination: any node-initiated egress NOT to a known registry/CDN host during install is exactly the payload-fetch / token-exfil pattern that motivated the v12 default change. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/using-npm/registry
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Telemetry beacons from npm itself (npm.community / update notifier) — add to allowlist
  • Long-running node-based apps (Electron, Slack, VS Code) on dev workstations — scope to npm-install windows
  • Internal package mirrors (Verdaccio, Artifactory, Nexus) — add hostnames to RegistryHosts
  • Postinstall steps that legitimately fetch prebuilt binaries (sharp from Cloudfront, prebuild-install from GitHub releases — pre-approve via the approve-scripts workflow)
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("github.io","prebuilt-binaries","verdaccio","artifactory","nexus"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the destination (IP + URL) and resolve it against threat intel (VirusTotal, abuse.ch, OTX); look up Whois/passive DNS for newly-registered domains. Correlate with the package being installed at the same minute on the host (lockfile diff or shell history). 2) Contain: kill the install, isolate the host, rotate any token in ~/.npmrc, GH_TOKEN, AWS creds. Add the destination to the corporate denylist. 3) Hunt: pivot the SHA256 of any payload dropped to disk into AlertEvidence; search the fleet for other hosts that contacted the same RemoteIP from node.exe in the past 30 days.
let RegistryHosts = dynamic([
    "registry.npmjs.org","registry.npmmirror.com","registry.yarnpkg.com",
    "npmjs.com","www.npmjs.com","npmjs.org",
    "objects.githubusercontent.com","codeload.github.com"
]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe")
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (443, 80, 4443, 8443)
| extend Host = tolower(coalesce(RemoteUrl, ""))
| where isempty(Host) or not(Host has_any (RegistryHosts))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let RegistryHosts = dynamic([
    "registry.npmjs.org","registry.npmmirror.com","registry.yarnpkg.com",
    "npmjs.com","www.npmjs.com","npmjs.org",
    "objects.githubusercontent.com","codeload.github.com"
]);
let NpmHosts = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe")
    | project HostStart=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound"
| where DstPortNumber in (443, 80, 4443, 8443)
| extend DstLower = tolower(coalesce(DstHostname, ""))
| where isempty(DstLower) or not(DstLower has_any (RegistryHosts))
| join kind=inner NpmHosts on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (HostStart .. HostStart + 5m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber,
          NpmCommand = ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: node.exe outbound HTTPS to non-registry destination
id: 5f9b4a05-5555-4d55-9505-ee55ee55ee55
description: Detects node/npm initiating outbound HTTPS to a host that isn't an npm registry CDN — the post-execution payload-fetch or C2 step that a malicious install script would perform.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/11
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1041
  - attack.t1568
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_process:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.cmd'
      - '\npm.exe'
  selection_port:
    DestinationPort:
      - 443
      - 80
      - 4443
      - 8443
  filter_registry:
    DestinationHostname|contains:
      - 'registry.npmjs.org'
      - 'registry.yarnpkg.com'
      - 'registry.npmmirror.com'
      - 'npmjs.com'
      - 'codeload.github.com'
      - 'objects.githubusercontent.com'
  condition: selection_process and selection_port and not filter_registry
falsepositives:
  - Node-based apps making legitimate API calls — scope to short window after install start.
  - Private internal package mirrors (add to filter_registry).
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\npm.cmd OR *\npm.exe) @DestinationPort:(443 OR 80 OR 4443 OR 8443) -@DestinationHostname:(*registry.npmjs.org* OR *registry.yarnpkg.com* OR *registry.npmmirror.com* OR *npmjs.com* OR *codeload.github.com* OR *objects.githubusercontent.com*)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|npm)\.(exe|cmd)$/i
| RemotePort=443 OR RemotePort=80 OR RemotePort=4443 OR RemotePort=8443
| NOT regex("registry\\.npmjs\\.org|registry\\.yarnpkg\\.com|registry\\.npmmirror\\.com|npmjs\\.com|codeload\\.github\\.com|objects\\.githubusercontent\\.com", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|npm)\.(exe|cmd)$/i | NOT regex("npmjs|yarnpkg|github\\.com|githubusercontent\\.com", field=DomainName) | groupBy([aid, DomainName], function=count())}, field=aid)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe") All_Traffic.dest_port IN (443,80) NOT (All_Traffic.dest_host IN ("registry.npmjs.org","registry.npmmirror.com","registry.yarnpkg.com") OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*.npmjs.com" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*.cloudfront.net") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe") All_Traffic.dest_port IN (443,80) NOT (All_Traffic.dest_host IN ("registry.npmjs.org","registry.npmmirror.com","registry.yarnpkg.com") OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*.npmjs.com" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*.cloudfront.net") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/

date: 2026/05/02

    selection_parent:

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-10520 — Ivanti Sentry OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-11 1 use case 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

Ivanti Sentry (formerly known as MobileIron Sentry) contains an OS command injection vulnerability which could allow a remote unauthenticated user to achieve root-level remote code execution. This vulnerability can be successfully exploited in cases where the Sentry appliance is in an unmanaged state with its endpoints externally reachable. The use of mTLS with EPMM or restricted HTTPS access through Neurons for MDM makes interfaces inaccessible to external actors. Vendor: Ivanti, Product: Sentry. Federal patch due: 2026-06-14.

Baileys CVE-2026-48063 (message-spoof / state-sync corruption) — TVM-surfaced vulnerable package AIInstallation High
Surfaces hosts where Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management has catalogued CVE-2026-48063 against an installed Baileys package (npm:baileys or npm:@whiskeysockets/baileys) below the fixed versions 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12. This is the cleanest signal for Baileys-dependent Node.js services that are still exposed to the protocolMessage spoofing / app-state-sync corruption primitives. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact CVE ID (CVE-2026-48063) and named packages (baileys / @whiskeysockets/baileys). TVM is the authoritative inventory-to-CVE join — far higher fidelity than guessing version strings from file paths. Cross-checked GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg on github.com/advisories. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Lab/test hosts intentionally pinned to a vulnerable Baileys version for regression testing
  • Pre-production WhatsApp gateway awaiting a scheduled patch window
  • Air-gapped or end-of-life Node service where TVM still indexes the package but the host has no inbound exposure
  • Vendor appliance shipping with Baileys bundled where Defender flags it but the vendor controls patching
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "7.0.0-rc12" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "7.0.0-rc.12"
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "6.7.22" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "6.7.23"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm Baileys SoftwareVersion is genuinely below 6.7.22 or in the 7.0.0-rc.1..rc11 window (TVM occasionally lags vendor patches; pull the actual package.json from the host to validate). Identify whether the host is an externally reachable WhatsApp bot/gateway vs an internal dev box. Step 2 — Contain: for production WhatsApp-handling services, apply the workaround (drop messages.upsert events containing a requestId field and set shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false in socket config) and schedule emergency upgrade to >=6.7.22 or >=7.0.0-rc12. Step 3 — Hunt: across the estate, run UC2 (filesystem) and UC3 (process) to find Baileys deployments not yet seen by TVM, and audit any persisted chat history written in the past 30d for forged-message indicators (no application-side telemetry will give you a clean signal — review with the app owner).
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-48063"
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where SoftwareName has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys", "@whiskeysockets-baileys")
  ) on DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-48063"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Baileys package directory present on endpoint (< 6.7.22 / < 7.0.0-rc12) AIInstallation Medium
File-system hunt for the Baileys library footprint under node_modules — catches Node.js hosts running WhatsApp integrations even when Defender TVM hasn't catalogued the dependency yet (private packages, bundled dependencies, hosts outside the TVM scope). Bounds the surface area exposed to CVE-2026-48063 protocolMessage spoofing. Rationale: Anchors on the exact npm package paths named in the advisory (`baileys` and `@whiskeysockets/baileys`). Pivots on `package.json` writes inside `node_modules` so we catch the install moment (npm/yarn/pnpm dropping the file) rather than every read. Operators then offline-grep the on-disk package.json `version` field to confirm vuln range — Defender doesn't index file content. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstation with the library cloned for local testing — high signal-to-noise but legitimate
  • CI/CD build agent doing fresh `npm install` per build (will fire every build)
  • Container image scanning sandbox where Baileys is unpacked from a layer cache
  • Patched host that has just upgraded to >=6.7.22 / >=7.0.0-rc12 — write event fires but the host is no longer vulnerable
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\AppData\Local\Yarn\Cache\"
| where FolderPath !has @"\image-scan-sandbox\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: SSH/PSRemoting to the host and `cat <FolderPath>\package.json | findstr version` (or `jq .version`) to confirm version is in scope (< 6.7.22 or 7.0.0-rc.[1-11]). Identify the parent Node.js service (`npm ls baileys` from the project root, or trace the FolderPath up to the project root). Step 2 — Contain: if the project is a production WhatsApp gateway and version is vulnerable, raise change ticket to upgrade and apply the documented workaround (drop messages.upsert events with `requestId`; set `shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false`). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot DeviceId into UC3 to see whether a Node.js process actually loads this directory (vs orphan dep tree), and pull DeviceNetworkEvents from the host for connections to WhatsApp endpoints (`web.whatsapp.com`, `mmg.whatsapp.net`) to scope external exposure.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "package.json"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\baileys\", @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\", "/node_modules/baileys/", "/node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys/")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Writers = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 8) by DeviceId, DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "package.json"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\node_modules\baileys\", @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\", "/node_modules/baileys/", "/node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys/")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Writers = make_set(ActingProcessName, 8) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername
| order by LastSeen desc

Node.js process running Baileys library — vulnerable WhatsApp gateway scoping (CVE-2026-48063) AIInstallation Medium
Process-tree hunt for `node.exe` (or `node` on Linux) actively running with a Baileys library path in its command line or working directory. Combined with UC1/UC2 this confirms which hosts have a *live* exposure to the placeholderResendMessage / message.upsert spoofing primitive, not just dormant node_modules. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact npm package names appearing in a live Node runtime command line — confirms the vulnerable surface is *actually running*, not just unpacked. Pairing FileName=node.exe with `baileys` in cmdline is high-signal because legitimate users rarely type that string into a shell; it almost always means a bot/gateway service. Combine output with UC1 (TVM) to prioritise hosts where the linked version is also vulnerable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running the Baileys example scripts locally (`node example.js` from the cloned repo)
  • Jest / Mocha test runner executing Baileys integration tests in CI
  • Internal employee experimenting with a personal WhatsApp bot side-project on a corporate laptop
  • Background pm2 daemon respawning an already-known WhatsApp gateway (high run-count but expected)
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jest.exe", "mocha.exe", "node-test-runner.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--test"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: cross-join the host against UC1 (TVM) and UC2 (filesystem) — if the host has a vulnerable Baileys version AND a running node.exe with the library, it's a confirmed live exposure. Identify the project root from ProcessCommandLine and check whether the service is internet-reachable (DeviceNetworkEvents → public destinations for the same process). Step 2 — Contain: for production WhatsApp gateways still on a vulnerable version, ship the workaround patch (drop messages.upsert with `requestId`, set `shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false`) within the next deploy and queue the version upgrade. If the host is a developer laptop, route to the app team for prioritisation rather than IR. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot the AccountName/DeviceName into 30-day DeviceNetworkEvents for connections to `*.whatsapp.net` / `*.whatsapp.com` to scope which Baileys instances actually talk to WhatsApp servers (vs dormant code); these are the highest-priority upgrade targets.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "pm2.exe", "npm.cmd", "yarn.cmd", "pnpm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys", "@whiskeysockets\\baileys")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\baileys\", @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine), ParentBin = any(InitiatingProcessFileName), Runs = count() by DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "pm2.exe", "npm.cmd", "yarn.cmd", "pnpm.cmd")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys", "@whiskeysockets\\baileys")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleCmd = any(ActingProcessCommandLine), ParentBin = any(ParentProcessName), Runs = count() by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48063")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Outbound TLS banner-grab scan fanout from single external SOHO IP · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2026-35616 edge-device exploit attempts from SOHO/residential IP space · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] MIPS-architecture binary download to SOHO/IoT device subnets
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound Tor connections from internal SOHO/IoT device subnets · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CVE-2026-35616 edge-device exploit attempts from SOHO/residential IP space AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for inbound exploitation attempts against edge devices (routers, firewalls, NVRs) leveraging CVE-2026-35616 — the vulnerability JDY weaponizes within hours of disclosure. Targets ingress traffic to administrative interfaces of Cisco RV320/RV325, Araknis, Mimosa, Ubiquiti, Draytek, Hikvision and Linksys appliances from previously-unseen residential/SOHO source IPs that match the botnet's geographic profile (US/BR/EU/Asia). Rationale: Pivot is the article-specific CVE-2026-35616 plus the explicit device list (Cisco RV320/RV325, Araknis, Mimosa, Ubiquiti, Draytek, Hikvision, Linksys) and the article's statement that JDY weaponizes 'within hours of disclosure'. Cross-checked against Lumen Black Lotus Labs JDY/KV-botnet reporting and CISA Volt Typhoon advisory (AA23-144A). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-144a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1017/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor management portal probes by ISP technicians
  • Authorized internet asset-discovery scans (Shadowserver, Censys, Shodan)
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) misclassified by source-IP geoip
  • Security research traffic from known scanner networks
  • Bug bounty researchers fuzzing edge appliances
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<known-vuln-scanner-ranges>") | where not(DeviceVendor =~ "Shadowserver" or SourceHostName has_any ("shadowserver","censys","shodan","rapid7","tenable"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the destination is an internet-facing edge device (router/firewall/NVR) in scope; pull SourceIP geo + ASN; check whether the device is patched for CVE-2026-35616 and whether the exploit pattern hit a vulnerable endpoint. Step 2 — Contain: if the SourceIP is residential/SOHO geo and the request reached a vulnerable interface, block the IP at the perimeter, isolate the edge device for forensic capture, and force credential rotation on the appliance. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the SourceIP across 30 days for any other reachable edge devices; pull device shell history, look for the shell-script dropper (`/tmp/*.sh` with curl/wget to Tor-fronted URL) and MIPS/MIPSEL ELF download; export `iptables`/firewall logs from the device.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionSuccess")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where LocalPort in (80,443,8080,8443,8000,8888,4443,7547)
| summarize ConnCount = count(), DistinctTargets = dcount(DeviceId), TargetSample = make_set(DeviceName, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP
| where DistinctTargets >= 3 and ConnCount >= 10
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor in~ ("Cisco","Palo Alto Networks","Fortinet","Check Point","Snort","Suricata")
| where DeviceAction !in~ ("deny","drop","reject","block")
| where DestinationPort in (80,443,8080,8443,8000,8888,4443,7547)
| where RequestURL has_any ("cgi-bin","HNAP1","goform","ISAPI/Security","luci","login.cgi","mainfunction.cgi")
   or Activity has "CVE-2026-35616"
   or DeviceEventClassID has "CVE-2026-35616"
| summarize Hits = count(), VictimCount = dcount(DestinationIP), VictimSample = make_set(DestinationHostName, 10), URLs = make_set(RequestURL, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP
| where VictimCount >= 3
| order by VictimCount desc
source:(cloudtrail OR aws.waf OR cisco.firepower OR fortinet OR paloalto) (@http.url_details.path:(*/cgi-bin/* OR */HNAP1/* OR */goform/* OR */ISAPI/Security/* OR */luci OR */login.cgi OR */mainfunction.cgi) OR @cve.id:CVE-2026-35616) @network.client.geoip.connection.type:(residential OR cellular)
# log group: /aws/waf/edgewaf-frontdoor
fields @timestamp, httpRequest.uri, httpRequest.clientIp, httpRequest.country, action, terminatingRuleId
| filter (httpRequest.uri like /cgi-bin/ or httpRequest.uri like /HNAP1/ or httpRequest.uri like /goform/ or httpRequest.uri like /ISAPI\/Security/ or httpRequest.uri like /luci/ or httpRequest.uri like /mainfunction\.cgi/ or terminatingRuleId like /CVE-2026-35616/i)
      and action = "ALLOW"
| stats count(*) as hits, count_distinct(httpRequest.uri) as path_variety by httpRequest.clientIp, httpRequest.country
| filter hits >= 5
| sort hits desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents values(Web.dest) as dest values(Web.status) as status from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url IN ("*/cgi-bin/mainfunction.cgi*","*/HNAP1/*","*/goform/*","*ISAPI/Security/*","*/cgi-bin/luci*","*/login.cgi*") OR Web.http_user_agent IN ("*Mozilla/5.0 (compatible)*","*curl/*","*python-requests/*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where status<500 | stats values(url) as urls values(http_method) as methods dc(dest) as victim_count by src | where victim_count>=3

Outbound TLS banner-grab scan fanout from single external SOHO IP AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts for the JDY scan engine pattern — a single compromised SOHO/IoT node performing high-volume TCP/TLS connection attempts to widely-distributed external destinations to grab certificate banners and fingerprint services. The behaviour distinguishes industrialised reconnaissance from normal client browsing by sheer destination fan-out and the TLS-handshake-then-drop signature. Rationale: Article explicitly states the malware performs 'high-volume TCP, SSL, UDP, and ICMP-assisted probing' and 'captures responses (TLS certificates, metadata)' — banner-grab scanning is the named behaviour. Fan-out threshold of 100 distinct dests in 10 min separates this from any legit SOHO client. Cross-checked against Lumen JDY report and the broader KV-botnet TTP write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595/002/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1590 T1592.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mail servers connecting to many external MX hosts (SMTP on 465/993/995)
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys) — should be allowlisted
  • Threat-intel platform pull jobs hitting many TLS endpoints
  • CDN edge nodes / reverse proxies fronting many upstreams
  • Browser-based ad-tech beacons (rare to hit 100+ distinct in 10 min)
Suppression filter
| where not(SourceHostName has_any ("tenable","qualys","rapid7","shadowserver","censys","shodan")) | where not(DeviceVendor =~ "Exchange" or DestinationPort in (25,587))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the LocalIP (or SourceIP) device — is it a SOHO/IoT device (router, NVR, IP camera) or a known scanner/mail host? Pull the TLS targets — geographic + ASN spread of 100+ destinations in 10 min is the JDY signature. Step 2 — Contain: if device is IoT/SOHO, isolate from the corporate network, capture firmware image, block the device's outbound flow at the gateway. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the LocalIP for outbound Tor connections (next UC), MIPS binary downloads, and any inbound CVE-2026-35616 exploit attempts in the prior 7d that may have been the initial access vector.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionFailed")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (443,8443,993,995,465,8883,9443,4443)
| summarize Conns = count(), DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), TargetSample = make_set(RemoteIP, 15), DistinctPorts = dcount(RemotePort), TimeSpan = max(Timestamp) - min(Timestamp) by LocalIP, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctTargets >= 100 and TimeSpan < 10m
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","permit","pass","accept")
| where DestinationPort in (443,8443,993,995,465,8883,9443,4443)
| summarize Conns = count(), DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), TargetSample = make_set(DestinationIP, 15), DistinctPorts = dcount(DestinationPort), Window = max(TimeGenerated) - min(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, SourceHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctTargets >= 100 and Window < 10m
| order by DistinctTargets desc
source:(vpc_flow OR cisco.firepower OR fortinet OR paloalto) @network.client.port:(443 OR 8443 OR 993 OR 995 OR 465 OR 8883 OR 9443) @evt.outcome:(success OR allow)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=/^(443|8443|993|995|465|8883|9443)$/ | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, bin(_time, 10m)], function=[count(as=conns), count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=targets)]) | targets >= 100
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, bytes, action
| filter dstPort in [443, 8443, 993, 995, 465, 8883, 9443] and action = "ACCEPT"
| stats count(*) as conns, count_distinct(dstAddr) as targets by srcAddr, bin(10m)
| filter targets >= 100
| sort targets desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as ports dc(All_Traffic.dest) as distinct_dest dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_dest_ip values(All_Traffic.app) as apps from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.action=allowed AND All_Traffic.dest_port IN (443,8443,993,995,465,8883,9443) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_ip _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where distinct_dest_ip >= 200 | stats sum(count) as total_conns sum(distinct_dest_ip) as total_targets values(ports) as ports_seen by src_ip | sort - total_targets
Outbound Tor connections from internal SOHO/IoT device subnets AICommand & Control High
Hunts for Tor entry/relay connections originating from internal SOHO/IoT device VLANs — the article states JDY operators 'use Tor nodes to manage infected infrastructure, including both the command-and-control (C2) and payload servers'. Tor traffic from a printer/camera/router VLAN is high-fidelity botnet C2. Rationale: Article: 'operators use Tor nodes to manage infected infrastructure, including both the command-and-control (C2) and payload servers'. Tor port set (9001/9030/9050/9051/9150) is the canonical relay/SOCKS port range; combined with Defender's DeviceCategory pivot to IoT/printer/router this becomes a high-fidelity alert. Cross-checked against MITRE T1090.003 references and Tor Project relay docs. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/003/ • https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/ • https://metrics.torproject.org/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1071 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Privacy-conscious developer running Tor Browser on a corporate laptop (rare in SOHO/IoT VLAN)
  • Penetration-test or red-team C2 over Tor
  • Researcher running a Tor relay on a lab subnet
  • Legitimate dark-web monitoring tools (Recorded Future, DarkOwl) on a sanctioned host
  • ISP-provided home gateway running OpenWrt with Tor pkg installed by the homeowner
Suppression filter
| where SourceHostName !has_any ("redteam","pentest","research-","darkweb-monitor")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the source is in an IoT/SOHO/network-device VLAN (printer, camera, router, NAS — not a user workstation); validate the destination IP against fresh Tor consensus (check.torproject.org/exit-addresses or Onionoo). Step 2 — Contain: block the source MAC at the access switch, place the device in a quarantine VLAN, pull a firmware/RAM image if forensically relevant, and rotate any credentials the device held. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot the SourceIP for the article's TCP/SSL/UDP/ICMP scan fan-out pattern (UC2) and for inbound CVE-2026-35616 exploit attempts (UC1) in the prior 30 days that may have been the initial access vector; check for MIPS binaries on the device (UC4).
let TorPorts = dynamic([9001, 9030, 9050, 9051, 9150]);
let TorIndicators = ThreatIntelligenceIndicator
    | where ExpirationDateTime > now() and Active == true
    | where ThreatType has "Tor" or Description has_any ("tor exit","tor relay","tor entry")
    | distinct NetworkIP;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (TorPorts) or RemoteIP in (TorIndicators)
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, DeviceCategory, DeviceType, DeviceSubtype, Vendor, Model) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| where DeviceCategory in~ ("NetworkDevice","IoT","Printer","SmartFacility") or DeviceType in~ ("Router","AccessPoint","NAS","Camera","NetworkPrinter") or isempty(DeviceCategory)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceCategory, DeviceType, Vendor, Model, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let TorPorts = dynamic([9001, 9030, 9050, 9051, 9150]);
let TorIPs = ThreatIntelligenceIndicator
    | where ExpirationDateTime > now() and IsActive == true
    | where ThreatType has "Tor" or Description has_any ("tor exit","tor relay","tor entry") or Tags has "tor"
    | distinct NetworkIP;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","permit","pass","accept")
| where DestinationPort in (TorPorts) or DestinationIP in (TorIPs)
| summarize Conns = count(), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort, 10), Relays = make_set(DestinationIP, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, SourceHostName, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by Conns desc

MIPS-architecture binary download to SOHO/IoT device subnets AIInstallation High
Hunts for HTTP(S) downloads of MIPS/MIPSEL ELF binaries — the JDY dropper fetches an architecture-specific payload (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64) only on embedded devices. A MIPS ELF transiting to a network segment that hosts SOHO routers / IoT cameras is a high-fidelity install-stage indicator. Rationale: Article gives the EXACT architecture strings: 'mips, mips64, mipsel, or mipsel64' — these are unusual file names anywhere outside an embedded-device flash. Combined with the article's note that the shell-script dropper selects payload by architecture, a hit on this regex from a SOHO subnet is article-specific install-stage telemetry. Cross-checked against Lumen JDY report and historical Mirai/KV-botnet payload-server URLs. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004 T1027.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OpenWrt/DD-WRT firmware update server downloads to home routers managed by IT
  • Yocto/Buildroot CI pipelines pulling MIPS toolchain artifacts
  • Vendor firmware downloads from sanctioned update URLs (Mikrotik, Ubiquiti, Draytek)
  • Embedded-systems development team pulling cross-compiled binaries
  • Authorized IoT device provisioning servers
Suppression filter
| where DestinationHostName !has_any ("openwrt.org","ubnt.com","mikrotik.com","draytek.com","yoctoproject.org") | where SourceHostName !has_any ("build-","ci-","jenkins")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the destination subnet — is it a SOHO/IoT VLAN? Pull the full URL, hash the downloaded file if available, and check whether the FileOriginIP is on a known firmware-update CDN or unfamiliar hosting. Step 2 — Contain: block the FileOriginIP at the perimeter, isolate the receiving device, capture firmware/RAM image. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot the receiving device IP for the article's Tor C2 (UC3) and the high-fan-out scan pattern (UC2) over 30 days; pivot the FileOriginIP across the whole fleet for any other devices that fetched the same architecture-specific binary; submit the file SHA256 to VirusTotal and the IR malware sandbox.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)(mips64|mipsel64|mipsel|mips|armv[5-7]l?|aarch64|sh4|powerpc)(\.bin|\.elf|_le|_be)?$"
      or FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/")
      and FileName matches regex @"^[a-z0-9]{1,10}$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP, SHA256
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, DeviceCategory, DeviceType) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| where OSPlatform in~ ("Linux","Other") or DeviceCategory in~ ("NetworkDevice","IoT","Printer")
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","permit","pass","accept")
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)(mips64|mipsel64|mipsel|mips|armv[5-7]l?|aarch64|sh4|powerpc)(\.bin|\.elf|_le|_be)?(\?|$)"
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[a-z0-9]{1,12}\.(mips|mipsel|mips64|arm|elf|bin)$"
   or RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)/(bin|payload|payloads|arch)/(mips|mipsel|mips64|arm)"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, FileName, FileSize, ReceivedBytes, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Ivanti, Fortinet, and SAP Release Patches for Multiple Critical Vulnerabilities

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Fortinet, Ivanti, and SAP have released security updates to address multiple critical security vulnerabilities that could result in arbitrary code execution and information disclosure. The security flaw patched by Fortinet relates to a command injection vulnerability in FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI. It's tracked as CVE-2026-25089 (CVSS score: 9.1).
